subject: Mathematics

unit.unitTitle: Statistics: Tally Charts and Frequency Tables
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2! In this unit you will become a real data detective. Statistics is all about asking good questions, collecting information to answer them, and then organising that information so it tells a clear story. Every day the people around you gather data without even naming it. When Amina asks her class which drink they would like for the Eid party, when Yusuf counts how many goats come home each evening, or when Halima records how many customers visit the family stall at the Hargeisa market, they are all doing statistics.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Conduct simple investigations to answer a statistical question.
Record and organise data using a tally chart, grouping marks in fives.
Convert a tally chart into a frequency table.
Read and make a simple pictogram where one picture stands for one item.
Interpret data to find the most and least common results.
Work out totals and simple fractions from a set of data.
Make and test a conjecture using data you collect yourself.
Describe your data clearly using the right mathematical words.

concepts.title: What Is Statistics and Why We Collect Data
concepts.explanation:
How do you find things out? Very often, you ask a question and then find a way to gather information to answer it. That is exactly what statistics is. It begins with a question you truly want answered, such as “Which drink should we order for the class party?” or “Which sport is the most popular in our class?”

The information you gather is called data. Data can be all sorts of things: the drinks your friends like, the number of goats in each family's herd, the colours of cars passing the masjid, or the weather on each day of the month. When you ask many people the same question and write down their answers, you are carrying out a survey.

Let us follow a real example. Imagine you are planning a party for your class and you want to know what drinks to order. You could ask everyone, “What is your favourite drink?” and write down each answer. But if you just scribble the answers in a long messy list, it becomes very hard to count them at the end. This is the problem that tally charts and frequency tables were invented to solve. They give your data a tidy home so you can read it at a glance.
concepts.example: Statistics always follows the same friendly path: ask a question, collect the data, organise it, and then read what it tells you. In this unit you will walk that whole path yourself, step by step. Once you can do it, you will start to notice questions everywhere -- and you will know exactly how to answer them with data instead of guessing.

concepts.title: Tally Charts and Tally Marks
concepts.explanation:
A tally chart is a way to collect data quickly while it is happening. It uses small marks called tally marks, and the clever part is that the marks are grouped in fives. Grouping in fives makes the marks much faster to count at the end, because you can count in fives instead of one at a time.

Here is exactly how tally marks work:

For 1 to 4, you draw single upright lines: | , || , ||| , ||||

For 5, you draw a line across the first four, making a gate of five (||||̸).

For 6 to 9, you start a new group next to the five: five and 1, five and 2, and so on.

For 10, you have two groups of five.

Think of each group of five as a little bundle, just like Sahra bundles ten counting sticks together at Nuur Academy. When you want the total, you count the bundles of five first -- 5, 10, 15 -- and then add on the few loose marks at the end. So a chart showing one full five and three extra marks is 5 + 3 = 8, and two fives with two extra marks is 5 + 5 + 2 = 12.

Why is this so useful? Imagine standing by the road counting cars as they pass. They go by quickly, and you cannot stop to write words or big numbers each time. A single tally mark takes only a moment to draw, and because they are grouped in fives you never lose your place. Tally charts are perfect for on-the-spot counting where speed matters.

A tally chart usually has clear labels down the side, one for each category you are counting. For a survey of favourite drinks the categories might be Water, Milk and Juice. Every time someone gives an answer, you add one tally mark in the correct row. Neat labels and tidy marks are the secret to a chart you can trust. Below is a completed tally chart for a survey of 20 learners about their favourite drink.
concepts.example: Reading the chart is easy now. Water has one five and two more, so 5 + 2 = 7. Milk has one five and four more, so 5 + 4 = 9. Juice has four single marks, so 4. Altogether 7 + 9 + 4 = 20 learners, which matches the number we surveyed -- a good sign that we counted carefully.

concepts.title: Frequency Tables
concepts.explanation:
Once your tally chart is complete, you can turn it into a frequency table. The word frequency simply means *how many times something happens*. A frequency table shows this count as a number instead of tally marks. This makes it very easy to read, because you no longer need to count the marks each time -- the number is right there in front of you.

To build a frequency table from a tally chart, you go row by row, count the tally marks, and write the total as a number. Here is the frequency table for our drinks survey, made from the tally chart above:

Notice how the frequency table holds exactly the same information as the tally chart, just in a tidier form. Seven learners chose water, nine chose milk, and four chose juice. A frequency table is like a clean copy you make after the busy job of collecting is done. The tally chart is for the collecting; the frequency table is for the reading and sharing.
concepts.example: So which drink should you order for the party? Milk was chosen by the most learners, so you would want plenty of milk. This is the whole point of statistics: you collected data, organised it neatly, and now the data helps you make a sensible decision. A guess might have been wrong, but the data gives you a real answer.

concepts.title: Reading a Pictogram
concepts.explanation:
There is one more friendly way to show data: the pictogram. A pictogram uses small pictures to stand for the things you counted. In a simple pictogram, one picture means one item. If you are showing how many goats each family owns, you might draw one small goat picture for each goat, all lined up in neat rows so they are easy to compare.

Suppose Idris makes a pictogram of the fruit sold at the family stall one morning. He draws one mango picture for each mango sold and one banana picture for each banana sold. If the mango row has 6 pictures and the banana row has 4 pictures, you can see straight away that more mangoes were sold, and that 6 + 4 = 10 pieces of fruit were sold in all. The longer the row of pictures, the greater the frequency.

Pictograms are lovely because you can *see* the answer without reading any numbers at all -- the tallest or longest row simply looks the biggest. To read a pictogram, you count the pictures in each row, just as you counted tally marks. To make one, you draw one neat picture for every item in that category. Always keep the pictures the same size and line them up carefully, or the chart can trick your eyes. A pictogram is really a cousin of the tally chart: both turn counting into something you can see at a glance.
concepts.example: Here is a small pictogram Zahra made of the goats owned by three families near Berbera, using one goat picture for each goat: the first family's row has 5 pictures, the second has 8, and the third has 3. Without doing any adding at all, your eyes tell you the second family has the most goats, because its row of pictures is the longest. If you do want a number, you simply count the pictures: 5, 8 and 3, which together make 16 goats. This is why pictograms are a friendly first chart for young data detectives -- they turn numbers into a picture you can read in a single glance, and they connect neatly to the tally charts and frequency tables you already know.

concepts.title: Interpreting Data
concepts.explanation:
Collecting and organising data is only half the job. The exciting part is interpreting it -- looking at the numbers and working out what they mean. When you interpret data you look beyond the numbers and answer real questions about them. Here are the questions a good data detective always asks:

Which category is the most common (has the highest frequency)?

Which category is the least common (has the lowest frequency)?

How many took part altogether (add up every frequency)?

How many chose this or that (add two frequencies together)?

How many more chose one thing than another (subtract)?

What fraction chose a certain category (that count out of the total)?

Let us practise on a real survey. A class of Stage 3 learners could not agree about which sport is the most popular, so they did a survey. Here is their frequency table:

Now we can answer questions by looking carefully. Which sport is the most popular? Football, with 12 -- the highest number. Which is the least popular? Tennis, with 5 -- the lowest number. How many chose swimming or tennis? We add the two frequencies: 8 + 5 = 13. How many took part altogether? We add every frequency: 12 + 8 + 5 + 7 = 32 learners. How many more chose football than tennis? We subtract: 12 − 5 = 7 more.

Fractions come from data too. If 32 learners took part and 8 chose swimming, then the fraction who chose swimming is 8 out of 32, written as 8/32. Working out a fraction is simple: the number who chose the category goes on top, and the total number of people goes on the bottom. This lets you describe your data in an even richer way -- not just “8 chose swimming” but “8 out of every 32 chose swimming.”
concepts.example: One warning that catches many young mathematicians: do not answer more than the data actually tells you. Our sports table tells us how many chose each sport, but it does not tell us *why* they chose it, or which sport they are best at, or whether they will still like it next year. A careful data detective only makes statements the data really supports, and says “I cannot tell that from this data” when a question goes too far.

concepts.title: Making and Testing Conjectures
concepts.explanation:
A conjecture is an idea about what you think will happen before you collect any data. It is a thoughtful guess. In statistics we love conjectures, because we can test them by collecting real data and then checking whether the data agrees.

Here is a famous example. You might think, “If I flip a coin 20 times, I will get more heads than tails.” That is a conjecture. To test it, you actually flip a coin 20 times and record each result with a tally mark under “Heads” or “Tails.” At the end you count the two rows and see whether your conjecture was right. Because coin flips are down to chance, you might get a different answer each time you try -- and that is a real and interesting discovery all by itself.

Another example uses a die. Omar throws a die 12 times and conjectures, “The die will land on each number twice.” He records his throws with tally marks, then counts. Almost always the die does not land on each number exactly twice, because these are chance throws. So his conjecture turns out to be wrong -- but being wrong is not a bad thing in statistics. Testing a conjecture and finding it wrong teaches you something true about the world.

The steps for testing any conjecture are always the same: state what you think will happen, collect the data with a tally chart, count the results, and then compare the data with your conjecture. Did the data agree with you or not? If you repeat the experiment, do you get the same result? Thinking this way -- guess, test, check -- is exactly how real scientists and mathematicians work.

You have now met six big ideas: what statistics is, tally charts, frequency tables, pictograms, interpreting data, and making and testing conjectures. These ideas are not separate islands -- they work together in one smooth journey. You start with a question, you collect the answers with a tally chart, you tidy them into a frequency table or a pictogram, and then you interpret the results to answer your question. Along the way you might have started with a conjecture and tested whether the data agreed.

Picture how this looks in real life. Khadija wants to know which fruit sells best at the family stall in Mombasa. Her conjecture is that mangoes sell best. She keeps a tally chart for a morning, adding one mark for each fruit sold. Afterwards she counts the marks and writes a frequency table. She sees that mangoes really did sell most, so her conjecture was right this time -- and now she knows to bring more mangoes tomorrow. That is statistics doing useful work for a real family.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to use them out loud with real things around your home. Survey your family about their favourite food. Tally the cars that pass during ten minutes. Record the weather each day for a week and make a frequency table at the end. Every time you do this, your data sense grows stronger, and reading charts and tables will start to feel as natural as reading words. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: How to make a tally chart
methods.example: How many marks are shown by two fives and three single marks?
steps: Write a label for each category down the side.
Each time you see an answer, add one tally mark in the correct row.
Group the marks in fives, drawing the fifth across the first four.
When you finish, count each row to find its total.

methods.title: How to turn a tally chart into a frequency table
methods.example: Show the number 7 as a tally.
steps: Look at the first row of tally marks.
Count the fives first, then add the leftover single marks.
Write that total as a number in the frequency column.
Repeat for every row.

methods.title: How to interpret a frequency table
methods.example: A fruit survey has these tallies: Apples one five and two more, Bananas two fives and two more, Oranges one five. Write the frequency table.
steps: Find the highest number for the most common category.
Find the lowest number for the least common category.
Add every frequency to find the total.
For a fraction, put the count on top and the total on the bottom.

methods.title: Find the total surveyed
methods.example: A tally chart shows 9 learners like apples and 7 like bananas. How many learners were surveyed in total?
steps: Add the two frequencies: 9 + 7 = 16 learners.
To find how many took part altogether, you always add up every category.
Check by counting every learner in the table once and confirming the total is 16.

methods.title: Most and least popular
methods.example: A sports frequency table shows Football 12, Swimming 8, Tennis 5, Basketball 7. Which sport is most popular and which is least popular?
steps: The most popular is the one with the highest frequency: Football with 12.
The least popular is the one with the lowest frequency: Tennis with 5.
Reading a frequency table means comparing the numbers.

methods.title: Add two categories
methods.example: Using the same sports table, how many learners chose swimming or basketball?
steps: “Or” means add the two frequencies together: 8 + 7 = 15 learners chose swimming or basketball.
Find each named category's frequency in the table before adding them.
Check your total by adding the two frequencies in the opposite order.

workedExamples.title: Count the tally marks
workedExamples.prompt: How many marks are shown by two fives and three single marks?
workedExamples.solution: Count the fives first: 5 and 5 make 10. Then add the three loose marks: 10 + 3 = 13. Counting the fives before the singles is the fast, safe way.

workedExamples.title: Draw the right tally
workedExamples.prompt: Show the number 7 as a tally.
workedExamples.solution: Seven is one group of five and two more single marks: ||||̸ ||. That is 5 + 2 = 7. Remember that the fifth mark goes across the first four to make the group of five.

workedExamples.title: Tally chart to frequency table
workedExamples.prompt: A fruit survey has these tallies: Apples one five and two more, Bananas two fives and two more, Oranges one five. Write the frequency table.
workedExamples.solution: Apples = 5 + 2 = 7. Bananas = 5 + 5 + 2 = 12. Oranges = 5. So the frequency table reads Apples 7, Bananas 12, Oranges 5. We simply counted each row and wrote the total as a number.

workedExamples.title: Find the total surveyed
workedExamples.prompt: A tally chart shows 9 learners like apples and 7 like bananas. How many learners were surveyed in total?
workedExamples.solution: Add the two frequencies: 9 + 7 = 16 learners. To find how many took part altogether, you always add up every category.

workedExamples.title: Most and least popular
workedExamples.prompt: A sports frequency table shows Football 12, Swimming 8, Tennis 5, Basketball 7. Which sport is most popular and which is least popular?
workedExamples.solution: The most popular is the one with the highest frequency: Football with 12. The least popular is the one with the lowest frequency: Tennis with 5. Reading a frequency table means comparing the numbers.

workedExamples.title: Add two categories
workedExamples.prompt: Using the same sports table, how many learners chose swimming or basketball?
workedExamples.solution: “Or” means add the two frequencies together: 8 + 7 = 15 learners chose swimming or basketball.

workedExamples.title: A fraction from data
workedExamples.prompt: In a survey of 28 learners, 5 chose strawberry ice cream. What fraction chose strawberry?
workedExamples.solution: The number who chose strawberry goes on top and the total goes on the bottom: 5/28. So 5 out of every 28 learners chose strawberry.

workedExamples.title: Test a conjecture
workedExamples.prompt: Amina flips a coin 20 times and conjectures there will be more heads than tails. Her tally shows Heads 9 and Tails 11. Was her conjecture right?
workedExamples.solution: Compare the counts: Heads 9, Tails 11. There were more tails than heads, so her conjecture was wrong this time. Because coin flips are chance, a different try might give a different result -- and that is a perfectly good thing to discover.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: Which sport was the most popular, and which was the least popular?
workedExamples.solution: Football was the most popular sport (12); Tennis was the least popular (5).

workedExamples.title: Combining two bars on a chart
workedExamples.prompt: How many learners chose swimming or tennis?
workedExamples.solution: Swimming (8) + Tennis (5) = 13 learners chose swimming or tennis.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: How many learners took part in the survey altogether?
workedExamples.solution: 12 + 8 + 5 + 7 = 32 learners took part in the survey altogether.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: How many more learners chose football than basketball?
workedExamples.solution: 12 − 7 = 5 more learners chose football than basketball.

activities.title: Coin Flip Investigation
activities.materials: a coin, paper, and a pencil.
steps: Make a conjecture: “If I flip a coin 20 times, there will be more heads than tails.” Write it down.
Make a tally chart with two rows: “Heads” and “Tails.”
Flip the coin 20 times and record each result with a tally mark.
Count the total for each row. Write two things you found out from your data.
Repeat the experiment. Did you get the same results? Was your conjecture right both times?

activities.title: Family Survey Project
steps: Think of a question to ask, such as “What is your favourite fruit?” or “What is your favourite prayer time to attend the masjid?”
Make a tally chart with a row for each possible answer.
Ask at least 10 people in your family or neighbourhood and record their answers with tally marks.
Convert your tally chart into a frequency table.
Write three things your data tells you, including the most and least popular answer.

activities.title: Ten-Minute Traffic Count
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a safe place to watch a road or path.
steps: Make a tally chart with rows for the things you will count, such as cars, buses, bicycles, and people walking.
Watch for exactly ten minutes and add one tally mark for each thing that passes.
Count the fives first, then the leftover marks, to find each total.
Which was the most common? Which was the least common? How many passed altogether?
Tally charts are perfect for this because things pass quickly and one mark is fast to draw.

activities.title: Make a Pictogram of Your Home
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and some colouring pencils.
steps: Choose something to count around your home, such as cups, spoons, or books.
Count how many there are in two or three different rooms.
Draw a pictogram: one small picture for each object, lined up neatly in a row for each room.
Which room had the most? You can see the answer just by looking at the longest row.

activities.title: Cereal Box Investigation (Think Like a Mathematician)
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and six differently coloured markers or crayons.
steps: Imagine a company gives one of six free gifts inside every packet, and each packet has a random gift.
Make a conjecture: how many packets do you think you need to buy to collect all six gifts?
Use the coloured markers to stand for the gifts. Close your eyes and pick one to be your “gift” each time.
Keep a tally of which gift you get, and count how many “packets” you needed to collect all six.
Repeat five times. What was the average number of packets needed? Was your conjecture close?

activities.title: Weather Watch (Week-Long Investigation)
steps: Make a tally chart with rows for Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy and Windy.
Each day for one week, add one tally mark for that day's weather.
At the end of the week, turn your tally chart into a frequency table.
Which weather was most common? Make a conjecture about next week and test it!

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand tally charts and frequency tables best? What was the trickiest part? Which of your conjectures turned out to be right, and which were wrong? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Tally Mark Rule
rules.text: Marks are grouped in fives. The fifth mark goes across the first four. To count, say the fives first (5, 10, 15) then add the leftover single marks.

rules.title: Frequency Rule
rules.text: Frequency means how many times something happens. A frequency table shows the same data as a tally chart, but as numbers.

rules.title: Interpreting Data Rule
rules.text: Most common = the highest frequency. Least common = the lowest frequency. Total = add every frequency. Fraction = the count on top, the total on the bottom.

questions.question: Amina wants to find out her class's favourite fruit. What should she do first to investigate this statistical question?

Only ask her best friend
Buy every kind of fruit

questions.explanation: A statistical investigation starts by asking a clear question and collecting data by asking everyone and recording their answers.

Only ask learners who like cats
Change his conjecture to match his guess

questions.explanation: A conjecture is tested by collecting real data and checking whether the data agrees with it.

Every sport was equally popular

The frequencies cannot be compared

questions.explanation: Describing data means comparing the frequencies clearly: Football (12) is highest and Tennis (5) is lowest.

I can record and organise data using a tally chart, grouping marks in fives.
I can convert a tally chart into a frequency table.
I can read and make a simple pictogram where one picture stands for one item.
I can interpret data to find the most and least common results.
I can work out totals and simple fractions from a set of data.
I can make and test a conjecture using data you collect yourself.
I can describe your data clearly using the right mathematical words.
